title: Malcolm X at Hajj
hook: he writes home from Mecca of pilgrims of every color in one brotherhood

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muslims in America: immigrants, African American Muslims and converts, three streams in one community. Your line was: american and muslim. Whose story did you hear? Today, one American Muslim's story. Day one thousand twenty-nine.

A tall American in two plain white cloths, the pilgrim's dress, sits down to write a letter home. He has spent years as the fiery voice of a movement in America, speaking hard words about race. Now he is in Mecca, and something in him is shifting. He has walked around the Ka'ba in a crowd from every part of the world. He has eaten from the same plate and slept on the same floor as men whose skin, he writes, ranged from the palest to the darkest. And he says he has never seen anything like it. Today: Malcolm X at Hajj.
screen: `TWO WHITE CLOTHS.` → `A LETTER HOME FROM MECCA.` → `THE SAME PLATE, THE SAME FLOOR.`

segments.voice: The man was Malcolm X, and his autobiography gives a chapter to the pilgrimage and the letters he wrote from it. He describes praying, eating and sleeping beside pilgrims of every color, and says the experience made him rethink much of what he had believed about race. He went home with a new name, El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz, and a new way of talking about people. What did he see? He saw the Hajj doing what it is built to do. Every pilgrim wears the same simple cloth. Every pilgrim faces the same House. In the rows of prayer, a rich man stands by a poor one and a king could stand by a farmer, heel to heel and shoulder to shoulder. The Qur'an sets human difference beside the sky and the earth: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours." Colors and languages as signs to wonder at, not ranks to climb. A saying reported from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in his farewell sermon makes a similar point: no Arab over a non-Arab, and no one of one color over another, except by mindfulness of God. Malcolm did not live long after. But the letter stayed, and so did the picture: every color, one row.
screen: `A LETTER FROM THE PILGRIMAGE.` · `A NEW NAME: EL-HAJJ MALIK EL-SHABAZZ.` · `THE SAME CLOTH, THE SAME HOUSE.` · `LANGUAGES AND COLORS, AMONG HIS SIGNS.` · then, large: `EVERY COLOR, ONE ROW.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about one brotherhood. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a time you stood or sat side by side with people very different from you, at a stadium, a funeral, a kitchen in a crisis, a prayer hall. What made the differences go quiet for a while? Then think of one person who seems other to you: different color, country, accent or faith. Picture them on your right, shoulder to shoulder, facing the same way. If you pray, you can ask God's blessing on them. The bell holds the time.
Malcolm X at Hajj. The pilgrimage that sent him home with a new name. Today's word, and the end of a week that went from the caliphate's end and partition to Britain and America.
Your line: every color, one row. Today, sit or stand next to someone you usually wouldn't, and say hello. Day one thousand twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Pilgrims on Hajj wear the same simple white garments, pray in shared rows and travel the same route together, and many Muslims speak of the pilgrimage as a lesson in the equality of believers.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's year (1964) is left out; no dates or ages given.

The Autobiography (published 1965) is under copyright: his letter is paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm the paraphrase (pilgrims ranging from palest to darkest skin, eating from the same plate, sleeping on the same floor, never having seen such brotherhood) is faithful.

'Says the experience made him rethink much of what he had believed about race' summarizes the letter; confirm it is fair and not overstated. His earlier role in the Nation of Islam is described only as 'the fiery voice of a movement'.
'Malcolm did not live long after' refers to his assassination; confirm the light touch is appropriate.
Farewell sermon hadith paraphrased and cited to Musnad Ahmad 23489; confirm the number and that 'white over black' is in that narration.
Pickthall 30:22 quoted; confirm exact wording (British 'colours' is Pickthall's spelling).
Week look-back (days 1023–1029) is folded into the word segment.

Editor: Qur'an 49:13 was quoted four days earlier (day 1025), so the teach, screen, match, myth, trapdoor and source now use Pickthall 30:22 (languages and colours among God's signs). The farewell-sermon paraphrase now says 'no one of one color over another, except by mindfulness of God', closer to the narration's 'red over black ... except by taqwa' than 'white over black ... by goodness'. The practice no longer tells the listener they have 'filed away' someone as other.
Audit: garbled carry phrase "someone you'd usually not" fixed; Pickthall 30:22 exact; Malcolm X paraphrase and Musnad Ahmad 23489 checked.
